#2082. Rangers icon Scott Arfield turns to Michael Beale after landing East Fife job

He broke through at Falkirk when John Hughes was in charge, played for five years under Sean Dyche at Burnley, helped Steven Gerrard to lift the Scottish title at Rangers, was a member of the Giovanni van Bronckhorst side that reached the Europa League final and starred as John McGlynn steered his first club back into the Premiership.

So Scott Arfield, who was officially unveiled as the new player-manager of William Hill League One outfit East Fife at New Bayview this afternoon, has no shortage of top-class coaches to turn to for advice about how to succeed in the dugout in the months ahead.

It was something of a surprise, then, when the midfielder revealed who he has contacted since agreeing to take over from the inimitable Dick Campbell in the Methil hotseat and who he hopes to emulate going forward.

“I have spoken to previous managers,” he said. “The one I have spoken to the most and as recently as last night is John Hughes. He has worked in part-time football before so he knows everything about it. I have known him since I was 15 and he has been giving me great pointers.

“But Michael Beale is definitely another one. He was the first person I spoke to when I got the job at Livingston (Arfield was appointed caretaker at Almondvale towards the end of last season). He is the same as John. He worked in academy football at Liverpool and Chelsea. He gave me an analysis.”

Beale, despite being first-team coach under Gerrard when Rangers were crowned Scottish champions for the first time in 10 years in 2021, is hardly held in high regard by fans of the Ibrox club these days.

The Englishman, who is now at Zulte Waregem in Belgium, struggled when he was manager in Govan and was sacked after less than a year in the role. However, he left a lasting impression on one player who became a firm favourite with supporters during his time with his boyhood heroes.

So what was it that Arfield liked about working with him? “His variety,” he said. “I was down at Burnley for five years, where they had a brilliant management team. But it was very structured in terms of Monday to Friday and how you prepared for games and debriefed a game.

“Mick perhaps didn’t have the reputation at that time. Steven was the authority figure. I wouldn’t say he was in the background as such. He was looking over things from a vantage point. But Mick was hands-on.

“His variability and ability to make everyone enthused and involved in the drill was just incredible. His knowledge of football and the variety of his training drills was amazing. It didn’t matter if you were a left-back or a centre-forward, everyone was all in, switched on and really focused on the training drills. That was my lasting impression.”

New East Fife player-manager Scott Arfield at New Bayview today (Image: Mark Runnacles / Shutterstock)

Arfield added, “He was absolutely delighted when I phoned him. He knows you cannot just go in at the top. There’s so many players who have gone from my position and even higher (into lower-tier teams). There’s very few players who can go straight in (at a high level).

“Look at Steven Gerrard, one of the most iconic footballers there’s ever been. He had to go into an academy at first. He was obviously willing to go into an academy and actually sit there looking at kids progressing. He got experience and then came up and won a league in Scotland with the help of Mick.

“Mick was delighted when I called him. He completely and utterly understands Scottish football at all levels because of the cup games we were involved in down the years. He knows it is a great situation. I think I am one of the first to get into management from that core group, so he is delighted to see it happen.”

Arfield also intends to get in touch with Gerrard, who took to Instagram yesterday to congratulate his former charge on his appointment at East Fife, in the coming days.

He admitted there are aspects of the legendary Liverpool and England captain’s management style that he will be borrowing in the weeks and months ahead.

"I certainly will be picking his brains,” he said. “I loved Steven's calmness as a manager. I absolutely loved it. When he spoke, people listened. I thought his demeanour was (fantastic).

“There were so many times he could have lost his head, but I think if you do that, if you're too emotional, players sometimes switch off, especially in this day and age. So the calm, authoritative figure is something that I'll be trying to keep.

“It does not matter at what level you are at, you need to get the best out of players. It is an important trait. It could be the most important thing you have got. I think I can get people on board and progress their football career and their ability.”

Arfield got a brief taste of management last season when he took over from Marvin Bartley at Livingston on an interim basis for the final three games of a difficult season. He was pleased to discover that he revelled in the position.

“I just loved everything about it,” he said. “I loved the chaos of it. I loved getting thrown into it. I have spoken to so many ex-players who have told me they thought they would want it and then when they got thrown into it found they didn’t want it.

Scott Arfield is unveiled as the new player-manager of East Fife (Image: Mark Runnacles / Shutterstock)

“It went the opposite way with me. It just ignited something in me that I knew was in there. But I didn’t know how big the fire was. When I was looking back over the summer at all these valuable experiences - dictating things, coming in at half-time and trying to assess the problems, seeing it from a completely different side from playing – I recognised that it ignited something in me.

“I was just waiting for the right opportunity. I didn’t want to rush into any opportunity, hence the reason why I am here in November. It is the perfect scenario and hopefully I can repay the faith that East Fife showed in me.”

Following in the footsteps of Campbell, one of the most successful lower-league managers in Scottish football history, will not be easy. But Arfield, who intends to play when he gets his match fitness and sharpness up to the required level, is undaunted by the prospect.

“I have never crossed paths with Dick,” he said. “But I have met loads of players throughout my career who have great stories about him. Listen, we have probably got different ideas about how the game should be played. But there is one ball and two goals.

“Belief in players is a big thing. You see it everywhere in Scottish football. If somebody can come in and give you a different dimension it is a good thing. There will be players here who will probably not be able to do what I am asking. They will find it tough. But I need to assess the team. Everybody is on a blank canvas.

“Whether they are good enough, whether I will need to bring players in in January to get to where I am wanting to go, we will see. The previous management team thought the players were good enough for their style. But it will be a different style.

“Obviously I will be telling the players what I demand and expect. But I will still tell them to play here how they would play with their mates – with that freedom. Football is an entertainment business and I want players to enjoy it.”

Arfield is optimistic that his contacts in the Scottish and English game, including at Rangers, will be invaluable to him if he feels that he has to strengthen his squad at East Fife during the January transfer window.

“I remember when I was at Falkirk first time around,” he said. “Yogi [Hughes] and Brian Rice at Falkirk travelled all about the country with not a big budget whatsoever. They were ducking and diving a bit like Del Boy to try and get the best deals. So that'll be my thought process, to recruit the best players.

“The best thing you can give young players is a platform to perform and get eyes on them. Under-23 football down the road and reserve team and B team football just doesn't quite give you what men's football gives you.

Scott Arfield is unveiled as the new player-manager of East Fife by chairman Liam Anderson (Image: Mark Runnacles / Shutterstock)

“So, that's obviously the scenario. That's why teams with high hopes for their prospects give them to teams like this - to put eyes on them and to get their talents growing at a faster rate than what they would get. I'll certainly be trying to use my contacts for the best players.”

Arfield continued, “We've got these Hearts boys (Connor Dow and Liam Walker) here, but they’re not getting enough eyes on them and they’re not growing. So Hearts are obviously going to be thinking, ‘Why are we giving you these players where we could just keep them training here?’.

“There's no obligation on me to play them, but they're at Hearts for a reason. They'll certainly have a point to prove with me. As I say, they're obviously there for a reason. Whether they can get up to a physicality to play in this league is a different matter.

“But the technical ability is there. That's another thing I need to look at - to see if they're good enough to put the current team out.”

#2081. 17-pass Liverpool player was ‘virtually anonymous’ v Fenerbahce; it’ll be a ‘concern’ for Iraola

One Liverpool player was accused of being ‘virtually anonymous’ in the Reds’ 3-2 defeat to Fenerbahce in the Champions League on Wednesday.

Andoni Iraola overhauled his attack for the game in Istanbul with a reshuffle which saw Bradley Barcola deployed in an unfamiliar centre-forward role as Alexander Isak began on the substitutes’ bench.

The Swedish marksman came on as part of a triple change in the 66th minute and scored with his first touch, but that goal would ultimately count for nothing as the home side struck twice more to secure victory.

Barcola stayed on the pitch for the full 90 minutes at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium, but his performance came in for criticism from Liverpool Echo reporter Paul Gorst.

The journalist gave the France international a lowly 4/10 in his post-match player ratings as he wrote: ‘Virtually anonymous in that centre-forward role that is unfamiliar to him. Glanced one header wide. Moved wide with 25 minutes to go but still struggled. This was a concern.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Iraola has shown that he likes his attackers to be flexible enough to play anywhere across the forward line, but the experiment of playing Barcola in the number 9 role didn’t work.

The Frenchman was unable to get on the end of a teasing cross from Joe Gomez in the way that a more natural poacher like Isak might’ve done, and he’ll feel that he should’ve done better with a glancing header shortly before half-time.

He did prompt one good save from Ederson after the interval, but on the whole the 24-year-old was disappointingly peripheral, as the figures below from Sofascore would suggest.

We fully expect Isak to be restored at centre-forward for the visit to Crystal Palace on Sunday, but it’ll be interesting to see whether Barcola reverts to a wide role or is omitted from the starting XI after a subdued display tonight.

On this evidence, we don’t envisage him being asked to lead the line again any time soon.

#2080. Virgil van Dijk is spot on: Liverpool's brittle defence leaves them looking like a vulnerable mess - it is unsustainable and MUST be fixed, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 12:00 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 17:38 EST, 5 November 2026

Liverpool's defensive woes are not sustainable, insists skipper Virgil van Dijk who says the team cannot accept losing in the way they did at Fenerbahce.

The Reds lost 3-2 having twice led in Istanbul, with individual errors and lapses in concentration costing them.

Andoni Iraola’s men have now suffered back-to-back defeats after also losing to Arsenal – and they have conceded three goals in each of their last three European games, against LASK, Villarreal and Fenerbahce.

When this statistic was put to Van Dijk, he said: ‘(Our defending) is definitely not sustainable. That’s why it is a very disappointing night, for many reasons but definitely the goals we conceded and the manner we conceded them as well. There is work to do.

‘It is very, very tough. Three set pieces as well. We have been very good at them so far this season but we switched off and were not ready for the first and second balls. Yeah, it is a tough one to take.

‘I mentioned after the last game, we as a group have to go through good moments but also lesser good moments. That will only form a bigger bond, it will be only beneficial.

Liverpool suffered a disappointing 3-2 Champions League loss to Fenerbahce on Wednesday

Captain Virgil van Dijk insisted Liverpool's poor defending is not 'sustainable' after the game

‘No one wants to lose games especially how we did today but it should only help us in the near future. We should not accept losing, especially in the manner we did today.’

Asked if he was angry, the Dutchman said: ‘Yes. But I didn’t show it today because everyone looked disappointed and they have a reason to be, they should be disappointed. We cannot lose in the manner we did today. But we did that and it is down to Fenerbahce as well.’

Van Dijk is right. The defence has been all over the place at times this season – especially in Europe.

Iraola thought he had won the game with a masterstroke triple substitution just after the hour mark when Cody Gakpo assisted Alexander Isak two minutes after the pair joined Florian Wirtz in entering the field.

But in trying to win the game – which is commendable – Iraola left the back door open. It felt ajar all night as Fenerbahce continually had joy down the flanks.

Van Dijk was asked if the deafening atmosphere of the Istanbul crowd played a part and said: ‘It is very difficult for everyone on the pitch because you can’t communicate easily.’

That could be an excuse but these players are world class and cannot put too much blame on the atmosphere.

Jeremy Jacquet has been imperious since joining from Rennes but the Frenchman had his first bad game in a Liverpool shirt, while Van Dijk was not too much better.

Milos Kerkez (above) and Kostas Tsimikas are proving a serious problem at left back

September 9: Liverpool 2-1 Atletico Madrid

Alisson, too, has left questions to be asked over his performances of late. After giving the ball away cheaply for Arsenal’s winner on Sunday, he was at fault for Fenerbahce’s decisive goal by dilly-dallying over whether to come for a cross. He should have gobbled it up.

But the real problem is at full back. Milos Kerkez and Kostas Tsimikas are not good enough – not now, anyway. That should be first on the priority list in future transfer windows.

Ronald Araujo, rested on the night, was missed.

The approach of ‘you can score, we will score more’ has been used – intentionally or not – in most European games this term. When it comes off, as it did in 6-3 and 4-3 wins over LASK and Villarreal respectively, it is exciting.

When it doesn’t, Liverpool just look a vulnerable mess. Work to do for Iraola ahead of a trip to Selhurst Park and Crystal Palace on Sunday, where Pierre Sage is fighting for his life.

#2079. Bayern were ready to pay £58.3m for Rio Ngumoha & may test Liverpool again

Rio Ngumoha’s future at Liverpool could be under threat next summer.

That’s because Bayern Munich reportedly remain ‘in talks’ with the young Englishman’s camp following a failed push to sign the winger this year.

Christian Falk reports for CF Bayern Insider that FC Bayern were prepared to put their money where their mouth is for the teenager in the summer.

A figure to the tune of €70m [£58.3m] was discussed, however, Liverpool’s uncompromising position on the matter meant that an alternative avenue in Ismael Saibari was instead prioritised.

“It is TRUE: Bayern Munich were prepared to pay €70m [£58.3m] for Rio Ngumoha. As we know, Bayern have been searching really hard for options on the left wing,” the head of sport at BILD said.

“We talked about Bradley Barcola, whom they were in contact with, and they were also in contact with Liverpool’s young talent. There were talks, his brother talked with FC Bayern, but it was a difficult situation for Bayern Munich. It was not clear if Liverpool would sell him or not. The price wouldn’t have been extremely high.

“So, you see, the club’s decision-makers feel he’d be a great option for Bayern Munich, which is why Ngumoha is still on Bayern’s shortlist. In the end, they had to decide for Ismael Saibari. Rio would have been complicated, so they just looked to seal the comparatively easier transfer of the two. Bayern are still in talks with Ngumoha’s camp, however, and he could be an option for the summer.”

You’d have to think Andoni Iraola and Co. will be pretty comfortable despite interest from abroad in Ngumoha’s services.

The player’s move to Anfield from Chelsea – which infuriated decision-makers over in the English capital at the time – was prompted by a desire for a clear pathway to the first team and developmental opportunities.

While the minutes are comparatively fewer and further between in the Premier League, the 18-year-old has been repeatedly trusted in Europe, racking up 285 minutes from a possible 360 in the Champions League. With 628 minutes picked up across all competitions in 2026/27, Rio Ngumoha is already well on course to blow last season’s total (1,065) out of the water.

READ MORE: ‘I like him a lot’ – Romelu Lukaku has been mindblown by Liverpool player he could face tonight

The other thing worth bearing in mind is this isn’t a manager throwing the left-sided winger out on the pitch willy-nilly. Andoni Iraola has shown a clear interest in developing Ngumoha into a more well-rounded, positionally versatile winger. After some initial struggles on the right flank, it’s already paying off.

Yes, at FC Bayern, the former Chelsea academy product would likely get plenty of minutes deputising for Luis Diaz in a less intense league, and the attraction of that possibility can’t be understated.

But if the ultimate goal is development and access to a pathway, he’s clearly already got that at Liverpool.

#2078. Andy Robertson set to scale Scotland’s Everest but King Kenny remains untouchable

Thursday is the 40th anniversary of Sir Kenny Dalglish winning his 102nd and final Scotland cap in a 3-0 win over Luxembourg at Hampden Park.

There was no formal announcement of a retirement afterwards. Paying a visit to the Dalglish family home in England, Andy Roxburgh asked the great man to help get him up and running as manager before focussing on his expanded role as player-boss of Liverpool.

At the age of 35, injuries were beginning to take hold and Dalglish had enough on his plate at Anfield without carrying the hopes of a nation on his shoulders as well. That night in November 1986 marked the end of the road.

It took four decades to reach a point where Andrew Robertson will match King Kenny’s record in Friday night’s Nations League game against North Macedonia. If he then plays against Switzerland on Monday he will move to 103 appearances and claim the crown as the most capped Scotland player of all time.

If someone has to topple the king then Robertson seems as good a candidate as any. Comparing players from different eras is always tricky and the Tottenham defender can do nothing about the fact that he plays in an age when players earn more caps than they did in the seventies or eighties.

Nor can he do anything about the fact that he plays left-back, a position which lacks the crowd wow of a goalscoring No.7 like Dalglish or John McGinn.

Brazil gave Cafu more games than Pele and if it’s good enough for the most successful nation in history, there should be no issue with Scotland handing more appearances to a full-back than we did to the most accomplished British attacker of all time. The achievement means the world to Robertson and his family and rightly so; they should savour the moment.

To children of the eighties like this one, the Dalglish cap haul felt like an Everest which would never be conquered; a record which never should be topped. Like retiring a shirt number in honour of a legendary player, it felt as if no one else should ever be allowed to surpass Scotland’s greatest player.

Kenny Dalglish (Image: Mark Leech/Offside)

Robertson would be the first to admit that the record will never make him the greatest Scotland player of all time because that’s a title which sticks with King Kenny. If Denis Law couldn’t pinch it, no one will.

Scoring 30 goals in dark blue and playing in three World Cups, Dalglish bore a talent which deserved that most overused of tags; that of the world-class player.

Not everyone thought so at the time, mind. Kenny was forever accused of performing better for Liverpool than he did for Scotland. Praise, and he received plenty, would be muttered through slightly gritted teeth.

The fulcrum in one of the greatest club sides of all time, he won six English league championships, three European Cups, an FA Cup, four League Cups and major honours as player-manager.

With Scotland, it was all about the moments. Rising to head home the goal against Wales which confirmed a place at the World Cup in Argentina. That quite magnificent individual strike against Belgium in 1982, his best, for me, and the thumping left-foot beauty against Spain in November 1984.

When he actually made it to the major tournaments, the dazzling smile which followed every goal was seen a little less than people would have liked. He struck in a memorable, if futile, win over the Dutch in 1978 and added another against New Zealand four years later.

For any player, scoring at back-to-back World Cup finals is a stamp of quality. His international goals total has only ever been matched by Law and, despite a valiant effort by John McGinn, that record will be harder to surpass than his cap tally.

If there is a ‘but’ attached to Kenny Dalglish, it’s the failure to lead the national team to the second stage of major international finals. Alas, the same asterisk can also be placed beside the name of Andrew Robertson.

John Clark's granddaughter opens up on bid to immortalise Lisbon Lion with statue

Ryan Jack knew Clement was doomed at Rangers as he reveals bad taste in his mouth

Morton may be struggling but charity is bringing hope to the community

Released by Celtic as a teenager for being too small, Robbo rebuilt his career at amateur Queen’s Park and then Dundee United, before winning two Premier League titles, a Champions League and a Club World Cup with Liverpool.

His nine years and 373 appearances at Anfield ended in the kind of tributes which feel like premature obituaries.

As an international player, he has driven the standards and culture which restored Scotland to two Euros and a first World Cup finals in 28 years.

It was Robertson’s idea to present players with personalised gift packs and handwritten notes before major tournaments.

On reaching the World Cup finals, his first thought was for his late Liverpool team-mate Diogo Jota.

Even if he never scores the kind of goals which make McGinn and Scott McTominay the darlings of the Tartan Army, his work rate, intensity and intelligence are the reasons managers love him and keep playing him.

Alex McLeish returned to manage the national team for a second time in February 2018 and made Robertson his skipper at the relatively young age of 24 after Scott Brown’s international retirement.

McLeish had won 77 caps over 13 years as a Scotland defender and knew what the role entailed. Describing Robertson as the ‘outstanding candidate’ and an ‘inspirational figure’, a leadership role at three major tournaments has vindicated that decision.

“By the end of this camp Andy should be above Kenny and I must be honest, I thought nobody would ever beat Kenny,” McLeish told Herald Sport.

Laughing, he adds: “It looks like Andy will and Kenny will be jealous of that.

“But I made Andy Scotland captain because he is a fantastic guy first and foremost.

“I could see that he was not scared to have a go at others and say, ‘hey, come on…’

“You need those qualities on the pitch and I think he is entitled to feel very proud of the footballer that he became after he joined Queen’s Park.

“He is a great fella, he has been a great captain, he has been a fantastic, ruthless winner in the club game as well. And, for me, Andy deserves everything that has come his way.”

Andy Robertson (right) in action for Scotland in 2014 (Image: Marcin Wziontek/Shutterstock)

The reality of professional football dictates that Robertson is 32 now and won’t be around much longer. The same might be said of McGinn and Ryan Christie and the group of players who have clawed Scotland back from the international wilderness.

When they go, it’s not clear who takes their place. Look at the under-21 team set to play Ukraine on Thursday and Aberdeen’s Mitchel Frame has played no first-team minutes this season. Bailey Rice of Kilmarnock has only managed 34 minutes since mid-September.

While the nation is still capable of producing proper players like Billy Gilmour, managers don’t seem to trust them enough to play first-team football.

Robertson derived the benefit of playing against men at an early age at Queen’s Park and then Dundee United and the same observation might be said of McGinn, Ryan Christie, Lewis Ferguson and Kieran Tierney. That’s how internationals are forged and right now the door is being slammed in the faces of the aspirational.

The lack of a first-team pathway for those aged between 16 and 21 is a ticking time bomb. A menace to the job prospects of Scotland managers of the future and of the here and now.

In a stark, if unsurprising, admission Sebastien Pocognoli spoke at the weekend of a lack of goalkeeper alternatives to Angus Gunn. Beyond Falkirk’s Scott Bain, Rangers reserve Liam Kelly and Jon McCracken, an English League One keeper, the cupboard is bare.

If the top clubs won’t play young players of their own accord, then they need to be incentivised or compelled to get their act together and, at a recent summit in St Andrews, SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland unveiled a package of measures to address the situation.

Five top-flight teams need more persuasion over the plans, forcing Mulholland to tweak the details to reach a point where they might have some chance of being voted through.

If they won’t fly at all, then the SFA may have to consider the nuclear option. The governing body have the option of changing the rules to make it harder for clubs to secure Governing Body Endorsements, which are required for visas, for the Joel van den Bergs and Kosta Nedeljkovics of this world.

A points-based system, similar to that utilised in England, would separate the wheat from the chaff and compel clubs to get with the programme.

Andy Robertson knows better than anyone how hard it is for young Scots to make it at a club like Celtic. It took hard work, perseverance and talent to make it after an early rejection and for that reason alone Scotland fans should turn up at Hampden on Friday to salute the man on the cusp of claiming Sir Kenny’s caps record.

Debating which of the two deserves to be Scotland’s most capped footballer, then, obscures the bigger and more important point.

In both cases, the cream rose to the top and unless clubs get serious about fixing the current crisis in youth development, it could be some time before the nation sees their likes again.

#2076. “It’s about ambition, concentration, desire” – Amorim tears into Milan after Ferencvaros defeat

AC Milan head coach Ruben Amorim did not hold back on his team’s performance after the 2-0 Europa League defeat to Ferencvaros.

Milan needed a win having lost two of their first three games in Europe, and instead they responded with perhaps their worst performance under Amorim. Lenny Joseph’s second-half brace was enough for Ferencvaros to emerge with three points that their performance merited in truth.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The decision was made to rotate again with six changes from the win over Inter, but in the second half the likes of Christian Pulisic, Diego Moreira, Mario Gila and Luka Modric all came on. The end result was the same: frustration and an inability to piece together the required quality.

Amorim spoke to Sky after Koni De Winter offered his opinion that it is a psychological issue for the team. The words from the manager were transcribed by MilanNews.

You issued a warning that today would be complication…

“There’s no explanation. There’s nothing I can say, especially about the first half. I don’t remember another first half like it. It’s about ambition, concentration, desire. We gave away opportunities, we gave away stupid gifts. We weren’t prepared to play football tonight.”

“It’s hard to explain. We simply weren’t ready to move from the derby to this other competition. When you play for Milan, you have a responsibility, and you can’t show up like that. I probably didn’t ensure the team took to the field ready either.”

De Winter says it’s a matter of mentality…

“We’re not ready to be competitive on two fronts. We need to work on our way of looking at football and how we approach matches. There are no excuses tonight, there’s nothing I can say.

“I usually have a lot to say in defence of our team, but not tonight. We need to be more humble and understand what happened.”

“Maybe I did something wrong these past two days, but not mentally. This team had similar problems last year. We have to find a solution. Tonight we weren’t ready, we weren’t brave. If we don’t win, we’ll have to do everything we can to turn things around, and we didn’t see that.

“Everyone needs to train like Pavlovic. He’s ready to die in training. He’s a good example. Sometimes when players don’t start, they struggle. But there are no excuses; we should have won even with those who started.”

“We have to fix this! We can’t just assume it’s going to be like this. We should have done so many things better tonight. Just being better on second balls would have been much better. We weren’t in the game tonight.”

How important is the Europa League now? It’s a complicated situation…

“I have to focus on the league, obviously, but we also have to do well in the Europa League. We must and can win games despite the rotation. We have to be ready – we’re not now – to play and win every three days.

“But I won’t give up on this competition. But as long as the mathematics don’t condemn us, we’ll fight in this competition as we do in the others.”

#2075. Liam Rosenior says Chelsea sacking had 'nothing to do with football' as he raises questions about 'tolerance' in England in first revelations about being axed just three months into the job

Published: 06:37 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:17 EST, 5 November 2026

Liam Rosenior has claimed he was treated unfairly during his doomed 106 days in charge of Chelsea, and that the way it ended in disaster had ‘nothing to do with football’.

Rosenior was relieved of his duties after losing five consecutive games without scoring. The fifth defeat in that run – a 3-0 loss at Brighton in which Chelsea did not even muster a shot on target – saw the players accused of downing tools to get rid of their head coach. He lasted 106 days in total.

However, Rosenior, now manager of Paris FC, who are fourth in France’s Ligue 1, has claimed his Stamford Bridge sacking was 'nothing to do with football' in a cryptic comment about 'tolerance' in English football.

The 42-year-old Englishman took aim at ‘the media’ in particular as he said in an interview with So Foot: ‘It was the best experience of my life, and the hardest, too. It was fantastic, even though it only lasted four months. I don’t want to go into details now. I’ll talk about it one day, when the time is right. But in a country where tolerance is an important value, what happened there has nothing to do with football.’

Pressed to explain, Rosenior continued: ‘I know, I answered without answering it. Actually, the moment that worried me the most was at the beginning, when we went through that five-game winning streak.

Liam Rosenior was seen passing a note to Alejandro Garnacho with Chelsea 8-2 down on aggregate against PSG - and the reaction to it clearly still rankles with him

Then-Chelsea manager Rosenior was compared to The Office star David Brent online

‘Any club would have been happy with such a run, but not Chelsea. You get good results and you’re in the spotlight. Then, there was a kind of snowball effect in the media.

‘They made fun of those instructions I gave (Alejandro) Garnacho on a scrap of paper when we were down to 10 men against PSG (during the second leg in March as they lost 8-2 on aggregate).

'The clothes I wore became a joke, the way I spoke, too. I’m not a joke! You’re the first people I’m talking to about this, and probably the last for a long time, but one day, I’ll tell you what really happened.’

It is unclear whether by ‘the media’, Rosenior meant those reporters who covered the club or social media, where he was routinely mocked and referred to as ‘LinkedIn Liam’.

Those within the actual Chelsea pack who attended Rosenior’s press conferences believe he was treated kindly despite the Blues boss not helping himself at times.

For example, his decision to suddenly drop Robert Sanchez for Filip Jorgensen backfired, especially in their Champions League last-16 first-leg loss away at PSG. When Jorgensen was then injured, Sanchez returned to the starting line-up with his confidence having been dented.

Rosenior also created a stir when he argued with a member of Arsenal’s support staff for encroaching in Chelsea’s half during their warm-up before the second leg of their Carabao Cup semi-final. He accused his opponents of breaking the ‘etiquettes in football’ afterwards.

After his players huddled around the referee Paul Tierney in the centre circle before a Premier League loss to Newcastle, Rosenior defended their pre-match routine. He described it as being designed to ‘respect the ball’ – words which were also ridiculed on social media, even if that idea did originate from Willie Isa, Chelsea’s hire from rugby league.

The former Strasbourg manager is now enjoying life back in France as manager of Paris FC

Rosenior added in his interview that he was never accepted in the Premier League, saying: ‘In England, there’s this preconceived notion of what a Premier League coach should be, how he should behave. You have to conform to that standard. People who know me know that I’m someone who tries to be sincere and authentic.

‘But I don’t have control over how the media describes me or talks about me. What I’ve understood now, and this is important for all coaches worldwide, is that social media, or the media in general, can dictate public opinion about the quality of a player or a coach.

‘This isn’t new, of course, but the biggest lesson from my time at Chelsea is knowing that they are also capable of constructing the entire narrative around a club’s trajectory.’

#2074. What Trey Nyoni did just before Alexander Isak goal isn’t getting enough attention

Trey Nyoni’s rise at Liverpool this season has been impressive.

The youngster’s potential was obvious to Andoni Iraola’s predecessor, Arne Slot, last term, but the club rightly decided to be careful with what was an 18-year-old footballer with limited senior experience.

It’s very much a different story in 2026/27, however, with the Basque head coach having already handed the midfielder over 600 minutes of action across the Premier League, Champions League and Carabao Cup.

If three consecutive starts for Liverpool – against Chelsea, Arsenal and Fenerbahce – doesn’t prove it, you have to think that the nature of Nyoni’s introduction against Crystal Palace more or less seals the view that Nyoni has become a key player for Iraola.

The correct decision was made ahead of time to rest the former Leicester City prodigy after a flurry of games, with our player of the season last year, Dominik Szoboszlai, restored to the starting XI.

But when it came time for the Hungarian to depart the pitch due to an injury concern, it was Trey Nyoni the manager turned to at the 69th minute mark. Yes, it’s worth pointing out that senior midfielders (other than Wataru Endo) aren’t exactly running amok on the Liverpool bench at this point in time. But this felt like a trusted substitution, a body Iraola has come to rely on, rather than one that just had to be made.

The assist credit will go to Florian Wirtz for the Alexander Isak goal close to full time, but it would be remiss of us to overlook Trey Nyoni’s contribution moments before.

The teenager can be spotted cutting out a low cross from Tyrick Mitchell in the box before picking out Alexander Isak (surrounded by three Palace players) further up the pitch. The ball plays out to Victor Munoz on the right flank, and Liverpool find a Palace defence in absolute disarray.

Isak strikes late on 💪🇸🇪 pic.twitter.com/J2fHbXlZyD

It’s not a fancy crossfield pass or Hollywood Gerrard ball, but there’s intention behind it, and it’s a positive use of the ball to help kickstart a Liverpool counter. Exactly what Andoni Iraola wants to see his midfielders doing at Liverpool on a frequent basis.

Ultimately, it’s so encouraging to see Nyoni continuing to be impactful in games even when he’s coming on, effectively, to see things out.

#2071. How Celtic fans can apply for new engagement group after supporter feedback

Celtic have opened applications for supporters to join the club’s new fan engagement group, Celtic Connect.

The initiative is designed to strengthen communication between the Parkhead hierarchy and the support, with members of the group set to hold regular discussions with the club’s senior leadership.

Celtic had previously announced plans to establish Celtic Connect before undertaking a consultation period with supporters.

Following feedback, the club have now made several changes to their original proposal, including increasing membership from nine to 11 and introducing a place specifically for a match-going supporter who does not hold a season ticket.

Season ticket holders selected for the group will also come from across Celtic Park rather than being categorised by individual stands.

Meetings will now take place four times per year, while a three-year sliding membership structure will see a third of the group change annually in an attempt to balance continuity with the introduction of fresh voices.

Celtic say the group will discuss areas including the club's strategic vision and objectives, its heritage and history, supporter engagement, stadium development and the matchday experience.

The debrief on Celtic's Mika Baur worry, Haissem Hassan omission & familiar problems Kasper Hogh has Celtic goal ripped away but earns something just as telling

Applications are now open, with supporters given until Monday, November 23 to apply.

"We are delighted today to open the application process for our new Fan Engagement model, Celtic Connect.

"The Club had recently announced the intention to launch Celtic Connect and following a period of consultation, applications are now open to join the group.

"Celtic Football Club is committed to strengthening its relationship with supporters and ensuring that fans have a meaningful voice through this new structure. Celtic Connect will provide a forum for supporters to engage in regular discussions and liaison with the Club’s senior leadership.

"In arriving at a proposed structure and remit, we reviewed the approach taken by many clubs elsewhere in Britain, and took advice from other clubs on what works and doesn’t work, in order to learn from their experiences.

"Additionally, across the past few weeks during our consultation period we received some interesting and important feedback from supporters.

"We sincerely thank all those who provided feedback and following this process and our own review, we have made the following changes to the initial proposals.

"The Celtic Connect team will now be increased from 9 to 11 members.

"Season ticket holding representatives will be selected from right across the stadium and not categorised from particular stands as previously discussed.

"We have added a position for a non-season ticket holding, but match-attending supporter as part of the membership.

"Frequency of meetings has been updated to four times per year.

"We have introduced a three-year sliding scale in terms of membership so that a third of the group will change on an annual basis to ensure fresh voices but also continuity.

"Throughout the consultation process, it was also pleasing to receive significant interest from numerous supporters wishing to join the Celtic Connect team. We will be contacting all these supporters directly to ensure they have the opportunity to complete the relevant application process.

"As we have previously outlined, Celtic Connect will consider:

"The Club’s strategic vision and objectives;

"Any proposals relating to Celtic’s heritage and history;

"Further plans for broader supporter engagement;

"Matters relating to stadium development, matchday experience and projects associated with Celtic Park;

"Relevant information sharing between club and supporters.

"We thank our supporters for their interest and involvement in this process so far and we look forward to updating our fans further on the progress of Celtic Connect.

"We would encourage all supporters to consider applying to be part of the group. The closing date for applications is Monday, November 23, 2026."

#2070. FC THUN 3 HEARTS 1: Vrancken's depleted side add insult to injuries with defensive horror show in Switzerland

Published: 17:40 EST, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:25 EST, 5 November 2026

HEARTS boss Wouter Vrancken admitted his injury-ravaged side were just not up to scratch as they succumbed to a bruising defeat that shattered any hopes they had of advancing in the Conference League.

Without the services of ten players through various ailments, Vrancken could have done without the calamitous defending that saw his side hand the surprise Swiss champions a first-half advantage they were never in danger of relinquishing.

First, Jamie McCart inexplicably poked the ball beyond goalkeeper Beau Reus in bizarre fashion when under little pressure from a long ball into the box after 22 minutes.

Thun went two in front 12 minutes later through striker Brighton Labeau after more poor defending, this time from skipper Stephen Kingsley.

The home side, who had lost their two opening fixtures in the league phase, added a third in the second half through striker Furkan Dursun and although defender Stuart Findlay reduced the deficit in the 82nd minute with a header, the truth was Hearts were well beaten.

The defeat leaves Vrancken’s men with one point out of nine following a 1-1 home draw against Nordsjaelland and a 2-0 defeat away to Trabzonspor.

Kingsley can't believe it after his poor clearance gifted Thun a second goal

Conceding his beleaguered team had shot themselves in the foot, Vrancken said: ‘Just not good enough. There are circumstances, but we expected more from ourselves. (We’re) Obviously disappointed.

‘Individual mistakes are always something that can happen because you are working with human beings. You have to find the energy again.

‘The quality was not top today. We don’t have to find excuses because the performance was not good enough. You have to adapt to the pitch.’

The Belgian also saw Kingsley, who has had his own fitness concerns recently, taken off with an injury to compound a miserable evening. He added: ‘He (Kingsley) wanted to play. This game was important and it’s always a risk.

‘It’s also a risk playing players who have played six or seven games in a row with two days in between. This is the situation we are in.’

Thick smoke from a pyro halted the game soon after kick-off but when play resumed after a lengthy delay — there were nine minutes added on at the end of the first half — Hearts winger Josh McPake drew a save from Niklas Steffen with an angled drive that lacked real power.

McCart bizarrely puts the ball into his own net to put the Swiss champions in front

McPake fired another effort at Steffen from 25 yards in the 20th minute after he had drifted in from the left, but his powerful shot but was beaten away by the Thun keeper.

There appeared to be nothing untoward on the horizon but then came a Hearts horror show. There was no real pressure on when a high ball came into the box but, with Lucien Dahler at his shoulder, a simple pass back from McCart somehow evaded Reus and slipped into the corner of the net.

Thun’s second goal was also gift-wrapped. The home side broke clear and with pace following a Hearts set-piece and when Nils Reichmuth crossed into the box from the right, Kingsley stuck out a leg to clear but the ball went straight to Labeau who swept it into the net from 10 yards out.

Dursun was shown a yellow card for a forearm challenge into the face of Findlay, and it perhaps deserved more punishment.

The interval gave the Tynecastle side time to reset but three minutes after the break Reus made a diving save from Dursun and an even better one from Reichmuth moments later.

However, the keeper was beaten once again when Dursun got his toe to a Reichmuth cross in the 56th minute.

Nico Maier raced clear of the Hearts defence minutes later and beat Reus with a chipped attempt that landed wide of the target.

The night got worse for the rattled visitors as Kingsley was replaced by 19-year-old Matthew Gillies, called back from a loan spell at Stenhousemuir.

Vrancken had to throw on teenager Gillies after Kingsley became the latest Hearts casualty

Hearts were sporadic in their threat. Malachi Fagan-Walcott’s header from a Jordi Altena free-kick was brilliantly saved by Steffen.

Thun had the ball in the net again after 78 minutes after Steffen tipped a free-kick from substitute Nassim Zoukit on to the bar but Jan Bamert’s follow-up was ruled offside.

Findlay headed in a consolation from another Altena free-kick but it was too little, too late, for a Hearts side who next face French giants Monaco at Tynecastle later this month.

#2069. “I’m really upset” – One thing hugely annoyed Andoni Iraola despite Liverpool win on Sunday

Andoni Iraola was left ‘really upset’ after Liverpool’s win over Crystal Palace on Sunday despite the positive, morale-boosting result for his team.

Having begun November with defeats to Arsenal and Fenerbahce, the Reds went to Selhurst Park in search of a pick-me-up in their final game prior to the international window, and they duly got in the form of a 3-1 victory.

Goals from Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak had the points secured well before a stoppage-time penalty when, in a clash of heads between Milos Kerkez and Dario Osorio, the Hungarian was deemed to be the perpetrator and referee Tony Harrington pointed to the spot.

Eddie Nketiah converted from 12 yards to deny Liverpool a fifth Premier League clean sheet of the campaign, and speaking to Sky Sports shortly after the final whistle, Iraola’s frustration over the awarding of the penalty was clear.

The Basque said: “I’m very upset [with] what they are calling in our box penalties, and the ones they’re not calling in the other box. I know that we are 3-0, it’s the 95th minute, but I’m very upset.

“It’s a head-to-head but even Osorio’s head, after touching the ball, is the one going to Milos. It’s not Milos to Osorio. A clash of heads.

“OK, you can say 3-0, 95 minutes, nothing happens, but for me there is more than this. There is more because it’s not the first time this season and you compare and I’m really upset, yes.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Thankfully the decision came at a point in the match where it had no bearing on the overall result, although we can still see why it put a dampener on the victory for Iraola.

To us, it seemed like a 50-50 contest between Kerkez and Osorio, with both players making a genuine attempt to win the ball and unfortunate to have clashed heads – most importantly, both were fine after the collision.

Harrington’s call didn’t have any major impact in the overall context of the day, but we take the Liverpool head coach’s point about the apparent inconsistency in terms of what referees deem to be a penalty and what they don’t.

There was certainly a far stronger case for a spot kick in our defeat to Arsenal last weekend when Jurrien Timber blatantly tugged Isak’s shirt inside the box, but somehow none of the officials on duty thought it was a foul.

It didn’t hurt the Reds yesterday, but hopefully on another occasion where there’s a stoppage-time penalty given in a game which is in the balance, we won’t end up having to talk about Iraola’s side being wronged by the referee and VAR.

#2067. Celtic board urge AGM rejection of 3 major shareholder demands including full apology

Celtic chiefs have urged shareholders to vote down a trio of proposals ahead of this year’s AGM.

Shareholders will gather at Celtic Park on December 1, with the board recommending they reject three of the four shareholder requisitions.

The meeting comes against a backdrop of discontent and unrest among sections of the Celtic support, with fan groups urging principal shareholder Dermot Desmond to attend.

And three of the resolutions set to go before shareholders cut to the heart of the current tensions surrounding the club.

The first calls on Celtic to undertake a full strategic review and publish a football, financial and strategic plan.

Interim chairman Brian Wilson has insisted work is already under way to modernise Celtic and address areas requiring improvement. However, the board will stop short of agreeing to the full review being demanded.

Read more: How Celtic fans can apply for new engagement group after supporter feedback

A second resolution calls for a full review of security operations at Celtic Park amid the continuing breakdown in relations between the club and the Green Brigade.

The ultras have been at loggerheads with the hierarchy over how they believe they have been treated, with relations souring further following a flashpoint last season which resulted in the group being banned after an incident involving police officers during the clash with Falkirk.

The third proposal demands that Celtic’s chairman issue a “full and unreserved apology” to shareholders and supporters.

But that was always set to be a non-starter. While the club acknowledges work has to be done, the board are urging shareholders to reject the call for an apology.

This year’s gathering also arrives 12 months on from a stormy AGM which saw Ross Desmond, son of principal shareholder Dermot, hit back at critics over the running of Celtic moments before then-chairman Peter Lawwell called time on proceedings.

#2065. Ronald Araujo agrees with Liverpool’s position on his £47m buy option

Liverpool would prefer to wait until the end of the season before deciding whether or not to activate Ronald Araujo’s £47m buy option.

That’s the claim coming out of SPORT, with the defender himself also understood to prefer delaying a decision until the summer.

According to the outlet in question, the Reds are thought to be “very pleased” with the Uruguayan international. However, the club is very aware of the fact that it will take a somewhat significant figure to bring the centre-back to Anfield on a permanent basis.

But barring a sudden, unexpected collapse of truly cosmic proportions, it’s difficult to see how Liverpool could manage to justify not activating the buy option come the summer.

Even if the club’s long-term plan is to use a less conservative option at right-back, the fact of the matter is they’re going to be quite short on centre-back options come the end of the season.

Club skipper Virgil van Dijk (contracted until 2027) may yet sign an extension, but we can’t see Joe Gomez staying put beyond the summer window. Either way, and even assuming that Giovanni Leoni returns from his ACL injury in excellent shape and has a significant second half of the season at L4, the Reds will need to bolster the department to the tune of potentially two bodies.

Activating Araujo’s buy option, then, feels like a necessity rather than a luxury, especially given the experience that could walk out of the door at the end of the campaign.

SPORT go on to claim that Araujo “is aware that Barcelona is keeping a close eye on him”, which doesn’t really communicate a great deal as far as intention is concerned.

Prior reporting has indicated that Barca boss Hansi Flick will hold some sway in the player’s next move this summer, but ultimately, it should be emphasised that Liverpool Football Club handed the footballer a new lease of life. Not Barcelona. And we’d like to think that’ll count for something in the long run.

Besiktas’ opener came from a bad kick-out. He does not look convincing with the ball at his feet and was lacking at the leveller.

#2063. GdS: A ‘true disaster’ – scrutiny intensifies as Milan sink to new low in Ferencvaros loss

AC Milan fell to a third Europa League defeat in four games last night at San Siro, losing against Ferencvaros who maintained their perfect start.

La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below) begin a report by asking the obvious question: what is the real Milan? Is it the aggressive, focused and at times dazzling side seen in the derby at the weekend, or the listless, disjointed, and sterile team witnessed yesterday against Ferencváros?

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In all likelihood, the real Milan are both – doomed, partly due to structural limitations, to oscillate between positive performances and lacklustre displays. To be clear, the Rossoneri won’t get far in any competition this way, as there can be no ambition without consistency.

Their last six matches have been a constant see-saw between victory and defeat. On only one of five occasions have Milan managed to come back from a deficit, a sign of a profound struggle to react.

Yesterday, their Europa League campaign became dangerously complicated: direct qualification for the next stage is now little more than a pipe dream, and even reaching the play-offs is hanging in the balance.

As things stand, Milan would be eliminated, and the schedule includes a daunting away trip to face Olympiacos and a home match against Sunderland, followed by two theoretically easier fixtures. The ‘Version A’ of Milan would have no trouble finishing in the top 24, but ‘Version B’ risks falling short.

One must also ask how much they truly care about the Europa League. While it is true that the squad lacks depth and injuries provide a valid excuse, Amorim’s team selections made it clear that Sunday’s away match in Genoa was considered the higher priority.

Yet, making such choices hinders growth. So far in Europe, the Diavolo have delivered three embarrassing performances in four games in Europe. It is a hard pill to swallow, but this is Milan: an international competition cannot be treated like a midweek friendly.

The match against a very good Ferencváros side was handled poorly: a terrible approach, an overly convoluted tactical set-up (even accounting for absences, which must be considered but do not justify such absolute mediocrity), and a complete lack of intensity.

It was as if the players were still suffering from a hangover following their derby celebrations. Amorim opted for a 4-2-3-1 formation, tasking Jashari with orchestrating play, while relying on the pace of Hutchinson and Cissé to disrupt the disciplined Hungarian defence.

The problem, however, was that there was no bow from which to launch those arrows. Jashari once again displayed a concerning lack of personality. Borbely assigned Bero to mark him, and that move alone was enough to reduce the Swiss player to performing only the most basic tasks, which he executed poorly.

Another issue in the build-up phase was the advanced positioning of Rabiot, who was drawn too far toward the final third, making him easy to shield. Unlike in the derby, he found himself receiving the ball with his back to the goal, almost always forcing him to pass backward.

Rabiot’s true value lies in his box-to-box quality: mobility is essential to maximizing his strengths, yet yesterday he was effectively caged by Amorim’s tactical design. Then there is Ramos, who touched the ball just three times (yes, three) in 30 minutes, despite the team holding 68% possession.

What is the point of maintaining possession if your best player remains on the periphery of the match and your centre-forward is never provided with a service? It was fortunate for Milan that, in the first half, Joseph displayed the worst of his repertoire, squandering two prime opportunities.

Realising the issues, Amorim tried to jolt the team into life by bringing on indispensable starters (Pulisic, Moreira and Gila) and dropping Rabiot deeper. It yielded no positive results, as the team’s build-up play remained predictable and their defense lacked cohesion.

Joseph made amends for his first-half finishing errors by scoring twice into an empty net. The first goal was gifted by a reckless back-pass from De Winter that Torriani failed to control; the second coming on a counter-attack, set up by an intelligent touch from Zachariassen.

Meanwhile, Milan’s first shot on target didn’t arrive until the 36th minute of the second half, courtesy of Hutchinson. By that point Ferencváros were down to ten men following Yusuf’s sending-off, and Amorim had deployed both Modrić and Camarda.

The coach opted for an improbable 4-2-4 formation with Moreira playing as a left-back. It was a move born of resignation, or rather, desperation. Which version of Milan will show up at Marassi on Sunday? It’s a question that naturally piques one’s curiosity.

#2062. Scotland hero tells Pocognoli the change Tartan Army are desperate to see

Robert Snodgrass reckons Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli should tap into the country's love affair with flying wingers as he continues to mould the national team in his image.

The former Scotland star accepts Pocognoli needs time to impose his ideas after succeeding Steve Clarke and believes the work between international camps will be crucial.

Pocognoli has favoured a 3-4-1-2 during the opening four games of his reign, a system which leaves little room for two out-and-out wingers. But Snodgrass would love to see Scotland eventually find a way of getting genuine wide men into the team and believes it could provide the attacking spark the Tartan Army crave.

Snodgrass, speaking to BOYLE Sports, who offer football odds, said: “It was a big decision him coming in. He hasn't started so well that people are completely sold on the formation and style giving immediate hope or suitability for the squad. That's the general feeling coming back from the first camp.

Read more: Next Aberdeen manager odds as frontunners emerge after Stephen Robinson sacked

“But he needs time to implement his ideas.

“A lot of international managers say they don't get enough time on the grass in international football.

“During the gaps between camps, your analysts need to reach out to players and share work. Take the time to meet up with key players, your right-backs, wingers, strikers, and go through the footage so that when the squad meets up, you're not starting from scratch.

“Meet them, show them the work and get these fresh ideas into their mindsets. They might already be doing that behind the scenes.

“When you step into the job, the workload increases as you try to get players comfortable with new concepts.

“When people feel an uncomfortable change, you have to put the work in so the lads feel it's simple, know their roles and believe in what we're trying to achieve. Once that happens, it creates belief within the squad that we're heading in the right direction.”

Snodgrass believes Pocognoli already has a solid platform to work from after the Clarke era. But the former winger naturally wants to see Scotland add another dimension higher up the pitch.

He added: “Momentum and positivity are key for Scotland. When they're in a good flow, you know Scotland will always be in games.

“They aren't expansive to the point of leaving themselves wide open, but are built off a solid base.

“That's a good starting point, but as confidence grows, I'd like to see us play with out-and-out wingers. They have Gannon-Doak, Josh McPake, lads who can go one-v-one and cause problems. I'd love to see that.

“It creates a spark and an atmosphere that Scotland fans are desperate for.

“We're used to good wingers in Scottish football. Being a winger myself, I might sound biased, but who doesn't want to see exciting, attacking football for Scotland?

“Steve Clarke built a strong defensive base, and the next challenge for the manager is to build on that by adding a real attacking style with players who can cause teams serious problems.”

And Snodgrass has a clear idea of who should be leading that attack.

Kieron Bowie has impressed and strengthened his case during the early stages of Pocognoli's reign, but Snodgrass reckons Oli McBurnie remains Scotland's best option through the middle.

McBurnie hasn't provided a glut of goals, but his performances across Pocognoli's opening four-game run appear to have changed the conversation around his international prospects.

Snodgrass said: “Oli McBurnie has proved he can score goals everywhere he's been. He's a great lad to have around the place, has matured a lot and has experience leading the line in the Premier League.

“Even in that game down to ten men against Switzerland, his performance was excellent. He showed everyone what he brings.

“In Scotland, we love a big number nine who can hold the ball up, attack crosses and link play. He has a lot in his armoury, so we need to stick with him.

“I feel for Bowie and the other young forwards, but having them come off the bench is a great option.

“Right now, leading the line in the Premier League gives Oli the edge, but Bowie and the others aren't far behind. They're three great attacking options for Scotland.

“They tried two up top, but it takes a few camps to realise what your best setup is.”

“I think we had a very slow start. I think we were mentally prepared: they showed us all the tactics, what we had to do and how to start.

#2060. Iraola admits uncertainty over Liverpool player’s international involvement after injury scare

Andoni Iraola has expressed concern as to whether one Liverpool player will link up with his country during this month’s international break.

The Reds go into the brief pause to the season off the back of a 3-1 victory at Crystal Palace, with some of the gloss from that result removed by a questionable stoppage-time penalty for the home side and an injury scare to Dominik Szoboszlai.

The 26-year-old pulled up towards the end of the first half at Selhurst Park on Sunday and played with a knee brace after the interval until he was substituted for Trey Nyoni in the 69th minute.

After the match, Iraola admitted that the Hungarian wasn’t operating at 100% yesterday, having only recently returned from a thigh issue.

The Basque said (via liverpoolfc.com): “I don’t know [if it’s] a problem, but he definitely wasn’t 100%. Let’s see. The last thing we need now is to lose players in the international games.

“Last time, in the international break, we lost three very important players, so now I’m praying – it’s the last thing we need.

“I think he extended a little bit the knee. It was fine, but not 100%, so he has to be careful to see if he can play with the national team or not. We will see, and also hope that it doesn’t happen like the other break where we lost Alex [Isak], Cody [Gakpo] and Dom. Touch wood we are in a better place in two weeks.”

On whether Szoboszlai would link up with the Hungary squad for their upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures, Iraola said: “I know he will do everything to go because he loves to play with the national team, but he was not 100% when he finished the game. I suppose they will have to analyse, the medical staff, and see what it is.

“I know what I want, but I also have to understand the national teams. I’m sure that Dom, if he is fine he will want to go, but I’m not sure if he’s going to be fine.”

Along with Iraola, Liverpool fans with no vested interest in the Hungary national team will surely be hoping that Szoboszlai rests up during the international window rather than representing his country.

Marco Rossi’s side are away to Georgia next Saturday and at home to Northern Ireland three days later, with promotion to League A well within their grasp heading into that double header.

As captain of his country, the midfielder will no doubt be striving to play his part over the coming week or so, but there must also be a duty towards the club which pays his wages and given him a platform to reach an even higher level in his career.

Liverpool resume their season in 13 days’ time with an Anfield grudge match against Manchester United, and they still have 11 more matches to play before the end of December, so managing players’ fitness will be vital during that relentless period.

Szoboszlai has been a frustrating figure at times this term, with debate raging as to where exactly his best position is on the pitch, but his creativity came to the fore in the win over Palace on Sunday.

Also, as he’s shown on several occasions, he possesses that X-factor to conjure up show-stopping and often result-altering goals.

Whatever decisions might be taken between Liverpool and Hungary, fingers crossed that our vice-captain is back to 100% for the Man United clash on the 22nd of this month.
